title: Mesoporous Silica Nanoplatforms: From Controllable Synthesis to Versatile Biomedical Applications.
abstract: The increasing global burden of severe diseases, such as cancers, cardiovascular and neurodegenerative disorders, highlights the urgent need for advanced diagnostic and therapeutic agents. Although techniques like computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography (PET), and chemotherapy show promise, their effectiveness is frequently constrained by the inherent drawbacks of conventional agents, such as poor solubility, low stability, and lack of targeting ability, as well as physiological barriers like the blood-brain barrier (BBB), which limit bioavailability and induce systemic toxicity. Mesoporous silica nanoparticles (MSNs) have emerged as promising platforms to overcome these challenges, offering high surface area, tunable pore size, and facile surface functionalization for efficient cargo loading. Therefore, in this work, the recent advances in the synthesis, structural control, and functional design of MSNs-based composites are systematically reviewed, with a focus on their biomedical applications in diagnosis (e.g., fluorescence imaging (FLI)/MRI/PET), therapy (e.g., chemo-, dynamic, thermal, and gas therapy), and tissue engineering. Key strategies for performance optimization and structure-property relationships are discussed in depth. Finally, we delineate prevailing challenges and future directions for the clinical translation of MSNs-based nanomaterials, providing an integrated perspective to guide their rational design and biomedical implementation.

title: Long-Term Disease Control Following Completion of Cladribine Treatment in Multiple Sclerosis: Extended Follow-Up of the CladStop Cohort.
abstract: Long-term disease control after the standard two-year cladribine course in multiple sclerosis (MS) remains insufficiently characterized in real-world settings. We evaluated disease control, treatment re-initiation, and safety during extended follow-up of the multicenter CladStop cohort after treatment completion. We included 204 patients with relapsing MS who completed the approved two-year cladribine regimen and had ≥ 6 months of follow-up after treatment completion. Time zero ("CladStop") was defined as 24 months after first cladribine dosing. Co-primary endpoints were time to loss of no evidence of disease activity (NEDA-3) and annualized relapse rate (ARR) after CladStop. Kaplan-Meier analyses, multivariable Cox models, and mixed-effects Poisson regression were applied. Mean follow-up after CladStop was 44.2 ± 8.6 months. Overall, 81/204 patients (39.7%) lost NEDA-3. NEDA-3 survival was 82.8% (95% CI 77.8-88.2) at 12 months, 69.6% (95% CI 63.6-76.2) at 24 months, and 56.4% (95% CI 49.2-64.8) at 48 months. Forty-two patients (20.6%) relapsed, with an overall ARR of 0.06 (95% CI 0.04-0.08). Relapse rates decreased over time (rate ratio/year 0.74, 95% CI 0.55-0.999; p = 0.044). MRI activity occurred in 29.9% of patients and 6-month confirmed disability progression in 7.4%. A new DMT was initiated in 40.7% of patients. Relapses during treatment predicted earlier DMT initiation. Disease control remained durable in many patients after completion of cladribine treatment. However, over 40% initiated subsequent DMT during follow-up, indicating that prolonged treatment-free remission is not universal. Disease reactivation was driven mainly by inflammatory activity rather than disability worsening.

title: Contralateral sentinel node drainage patterns in early lateralised oral squamous cell carcinoma - a retrospective study.
journal: The British journal of oral & maxillofacial surgery
abstract: Sentinel node biopsy (SNB) maps tumour draining lymph nodes on an individual basis, identifying locations outside typical neck dissection levels including the contralateral neck. We report contralateral drainage and positivity rates in lateralised early oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma (OCSCC) and assess associations with tumour characteristics. This was a single-centre retrospective study of patients with lateralised cT1-T2 OCSCC treated with wide local excision and SNB between February 2016 and January 2022. Data included tumour depth, distance to the midline, lymphatic drainage, sentinel node number/location and SNB status. Variables were analysed using two-tailed Student t-test and Fisher's exact test, with Holm-Bonferroni correction where appropriate. Ninety-two patients underwent SNB; 64 met the criteria for lymphatic drainage analysis. Contralateral or bilateral drainage occurred in 26 (40.6%) cases. Fifty (78.1%) tumours involved the anterior 2/3 tongue, with contralateral or bilateral drainage in 20 (40.0%). Twenty-two patients (34.4%) had positive SNB, including three (4.7%) with contralateral metastases. Mean follow up was 46.3 months. One- and 3-year overall survival were 93.7% and 77.8%, respectively; disease-free survival was 91.7% and 80.0%, respectively. One patient (1.5%) had a false-negative SNB, and three (4.7%) would have been inadequately staged or treated by ipsilateral elective neck dissection. Contralateral drainage was common in lateralised early OCSCC, although contralateral positivity was uncommon. SNB may improve individualised staging by identifying clinically relevant contralateral drainage not addressed by ipsilateral elective neck dissection. Prospective multicentre studies are needed to define anatomical and tumour-related predictive factors for contralateral drainage.

title: The Pharmacologic Management of Cardiac Arrest.
abstract: The effectiveness of pharmacologic management of cardiac arrest patients is widely debated; however, several studies published in the past 5 years have begun to clarify some of these issues. This article covers the current state of evidence for the effectiveness of the vasopressor epinephrine and the combination of vasopressin-steroids-epinephrine and antiarrhythmic medications amiodarone and lidocaine and reviews the role of other medications such as calcium, sodium bicarbonate, magnesium, and atropine in cardiac arrest care. We additionally review the role of β-blockers for refractory pulseless ventricular tachycardia/ventricular fibrillation and thrombolytics in undifferentiated cardiac arrest and suspected fatal pulmonary embolism.

title: Changes in Demographic and Clinical Characteristics of MuSK Myasthenia Gravis.
abstract: Over the last two decades, an increasing number of late- and very-late onset myasthenia gravis cases (VLOMG) with acetylcholine receptor antibodies (AChR-MG) have been reported, whereas demographic studies on muscle-specific tyrosine kinase antibodies MG (MuSK-MG) are lacking. We investigated whether the proportion of patients with MuSK-MG with onset ≥ 50 years has increased and whether these patients show distinct clinical characteristics. We retrospectively enrolled consecutive patients with MuSK-MG onset ≥ 16 years followed between 1980 and 2025 at our tertiary center. Demographic characteristics and maximum disease severity, classified according to Myasthenia Gravis Foundation of America classification, were analyzed. Patients were stratified into three age-at-onset subgroups. Overall, 120 patients were included. A significant increase in the median age at MuSK-MG onset was observed, from 36 years (IQR, 23-45.75) in the 1980s to 47 years (IQR, 29-69) in the 2013-2025 period (p = 0.033). Patients with onset ≥ 50 years increased from 2/17 (11.8%) to 19/39 (48.7%) (p = 0.015), including 12 VLOMG cases. Males increased from 23.5% to 35.9%. Maximum MG severity decreased over time, with a remarkable reduction of respiratory crises (p = 0.004), with no significant differences across age-at-onset groups. Demographic changes observed in AChR-MG also occur, though less prominently, in MuSK-MG.

title: Performance-Metacognition Dissociation During Fear Memory Recall: Role of Task Sequence and Prefrontal TMS.
abstract: Metacognitive processing-the ability to monitor and evaluate one's decisions-has been extensively studied in perceptual tasks but never examined in fear conditioning. We investigated whether metacognitive sensitivity can be quantified in emotional learning and how testing order and neuromodulation of the anterior prefrontal cortex (aPFC) influence metacognitive access to the memory of a shock-associated cue. Eighty-one participants (51 females and 30 males) underwent fear conditioning and received either active or sham TMS over the aPFC. They were tested with implicit (skin conductance) and explicit (two-interval forced-choice with confidence ratings) tasks in counterbalanced order. Behavioral performance (d') and metacognitive sensitivity (meta-d') were quantified using signal detection theory. While d' remained stable across conditions, meta-d' and confidence were significantly higher when the explicit task preceded the implicit task. TMS did not affect metacognitive sensitivity. To our knowledge, these results provide the first evidence that metacognitive frameworks can be applied to a fear-conditioning paradigm, revealing that confidence judgments are dynamically modulated by task sequence and remain intact even when bodily arousal is reduced. We propose that metacognitive sensitivity may decline faster than first-order performance, pointing to a functional dissociation between decision accuracy and metacognition in emotionally salient contexts.Significance Statement This study provides the first evidence that metacognitive monitoring can be quantified within a fear-conditioning paradigm, extending metacognitive research beyond perceptual decision-making into emotional learning. We show that confidence in recognizing a shock-associated cue can be dissociated from first-order performance: task sequence critically modulates metacognitive sensitivity even when first-order performance remains stable. Notably, confidence judgments persist despite reduced autonomic arousal following prefrontal stimulation, suggesting that metacognitive access does not require intact bodily signals. These findings indicate that fear conditioning offers a viable paradigm for investigating metacognition and suggest a partial dissociation between first-order performance and self-monitoring in emotional memory. This work opens new avenues for understanding confidence disruptions in anxiety disorders in which threat detection and metacognitive evaluation are impaired.

title: Targeting Response Regulator PprB Protein With Natural Compounds to Develop Novel Therapies Against Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
abstract: The pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa (P. aeruginosa) is recognized as an international pathogen of significance due to its multidrug resistance and strong ability to create biofilm as the basis of chronic and device-associated infections. The two-component regulatory system PprAB is important in the biofilm network, where the response regulator PprB regulates binding, aggregation, and biofilm production in the extracellular environment. The current research took PprB as a probable anti-biofilm target and assessed two biogenic ligands, atropine and α-ketoglutarate, as potential inhibitory substrates. PprB was purified and structural studies were conducted to investigate ligand-binding interactions and structural stability. Conserved regulatory motifs were identified through sequence analysis and multiple sequence alignments. Biofilm inhibition, combinatory assays, antimicrobial study, fluorescence spectroscopy, and FESEM were conducted to experimentally validate the interactions and functional analysis of PprB. Collectively, our findings highlight PprB as a promising therapeutic target and demonstrate the potential of atropine and α-ketoglutarate as effective modulators of P. aeruginosa biofilm formation.

title: Conservation of a synaptic blueprint across the animal kingdom.
abstract: Chemical synapses are fundamental computational units of the nervous system that enable rapid and precise information transfer through the nanoscale organization of presynaptic and postsynaptic components. Despite hundreds of millions of years of animal evolution and extraordinary diversity in nervous system architectures, the core physiological principles of chemical synaptic transmission remain remarkably conserved. Studies across Drosophila melanogaster, zebrafish, Caenorhabditis elegans, frogs and mammals reveal recurring principles governing active-zone organization, synaptic vesicle exocytosis, calcium signalling and postsynaptic specialization. Here, we examine the evolution of chemical synapses across the animal kingdom, focusing on the relationship between molecular diversification, nanoscale organization and functional conservation. We propose that the evolutionary stability of synapses reflects, in part, a stringent biophysical constraint imposed by the requirements for rapid chemical communication. We further consider how these conserved synaptic operations are assembled into neural circuits of dramatically different complexities, as well as the ctenophore nervous system as a critical test case for distinguishing molecular conservation from architectural and functional convergence. Across species, the emerging picture is that evolution has adhered to conserving the geometry and organizational principles of chemical synapses more stringently than a precise molecular composition. Synapses thus represent stable yet adaptable information-processing architectures in which conserved nanoscale constraints coexist with molecular flexibility and extensive diversification of neural circuits.

title: Management of Chronic Subdural Hematoma in Thrombocytopenia: Middle Meningeal Artery Embolization - Based Strategies Versus Medical Management or Surgery Alone.
abstract: Thrombocytopenia complicates management of chronic subdural hematoma (cSDH), but no study has compared middle meningeal artery embolization (MMAE) with surgery or medical management in this population. We evaluated MMAE-containing strategies versus medical management or surgery alone in cSDH with platelets below 100×103/µL. Using the TriNetX Research Network, we identified adults with cSDH and platelets below 100×103/µL (or below 50×103/µL for the severe-thrombocytopenia analysis). We performed three propensity-score-matched comparisons: standalone MMAE versus medical management and surgery plus MMAE versus surgery alone at platelets <100×103/µL; and standalone MMAE versus medical management at platelets <50×103/µL. The primary outcome was 90-day all-cause mortality; the secondary outcome was surgical evacuation (a composite of surgical evacuation or mortality at platelets <50×103/µL). After matching, cohorts ranged from 147 to 373 patients per group (standardized mean differences below 0.10 for nearly all covariates). At platelets <100×103/µL, standalone MMAE was associated with lower mortality than medical management (26.9% vs 37.3% hazard ratio 0.65 [95% CI 0.50-0.85]), and surgery plus MMAE was associated with lower mortality than surgery alone (20.5% vs 30.7%; hazard ratio 0.61 [95% CI 0.38-0.97]). At platelets <50×103/µL, the mortality comparison between standalone MMAE and medical management did not reach significance (34.2% vs 44.0%; hazard ratio 0.72 [95% CI 0.49-1.05]). Subsequent surgical evacuation did not differ significantly in any comparison. For patients with cSDH and thrombocytopenia, management strategies incorporating MMAE were associated with lower 90-day mortality than medical management or surgery alone. Prospective confirmation is needed, including in severe thrombocytopenia, where the mortality comparison did not reach significance.

title: Serious Adverse Events in Adult ICU Patients: A Substudy of the PATIENCE Cohort.
abstract: Prokinetic agents are used to enhance upper gastrointestinal motility, but adverse events related to these agents are poorly described. We aimed to provide detailed epidemiological data on predefined serious adverse events (SAEs) in a cohort of adult intensive care unit (ICU) patients with and without prokinetic treatment. We hypothesised that all predefined SAEs would occur in both patients treated and those not treated with prokinetic agents, and that a higher number of SAEs would occur among patients treated with prokinetic agents for more than three consecutive days. This substudy of the inception cohort study "Prokinetic agents in adult intensive care unit patients" included acutely admitted adult ICU patients. The prokinetic agents assessed (exposures) were erythromycin, metoclopramide, domperidone, and prucalopride. The primary outcome was the proportion of patients experiencing at least one episode of five pre-specified SAEs during ICU stay (cardiac arrhythmias, cardiac arrest, vomiting with aspiration, diarrhoea, extrapyramidal symptoms). Secondary outcomes were (1) proportion of patients experiencing each SAE, (2) the proportion of patients experiencing any of the SAEs after prokinetic treatment stratified by longest consecutive treatment duration, (3) time from index ICU admission to first SAE and (4) time from prokinetic initiation to first SAE. All analyses were descriptive, summarising SAE proportions and timing overall and according to prokinetic exposure. Among 1440 adult ICU patients, 710 SAEs occurred in 354 patients (24.6%), most commonly cardiac arrhythmias (199/1440, 13.8%). Across the exposure groups, the proportion of patients experiencing one or more SAEs ranged from 23.0% to 42.5%. Among patients treated with prokinetic agents for > 3 consecutive days, 14/59 (23.7%) experienced a SAE, which was similar to the proportion observed among patients not receiving prokinetic agents (291/1.253, 23.2%). Most SAEs occurred on median Day 2 after ICU admission and on median Day 3 after prokinetic initiation. One in four adult ICU patients experienced at least one SAE, with cardiac arrhythmias being the most frequent. Among patients receiving prokinetic agents, the proportion experiencing one or more SAEs ranged from 23.0% to 42.5% across treatment groups. The findings from this study may help inform the design of a future clinical trial. This analysis presents reported serious adverse event observed in an ICU trial cohort assessing gastrointestinal prokinetic drug effects. Serious adverse events were reported frequently in both the drug treatment groups and the comparison (no prokinetic drug) group. Types of serious adverse events reported are presented.

title: Memory reactivation alters the fate of neutral episodic memories following a subsequent independent experience.
abstract: Memory reactivation may lead to strengthening, weakening, or updating depending on the experience that follows retrieval. Although post-reactivation modification has been shown for emotional, aversive, and naturalistic episodic memories, it remains unclear whether a consolidated neutral memory for an everyday-like event can be distorted when reactivation is followed by a subsequent independent episodic experience. Yet memories that later become relevant for testimony often initially concern neutral everyday events, such as conversations, routine encounters, or the presence of a person in a given context. Here, we examined whether a consolidated complex neutral episodic memory could be modified when reactivation was followed by a subsequent independent episodic experience. Participants encoded a neutral audiovisual story and returned one week later for an incomplete reminder designed to reactivate the original memory. After reactivation, one group encoded a second neutral audiovisual story, whereas another group received the reminder only. Two control groups either encoded the second story without prior reactivation or received no reminder. One week later, memory was assessed using free recall, cued recall, recognition, and temporal order tasks. Exposure to the second episodic experience was associated with reduced accurate recall and increased memory distortions. Critically, participants whose original memory was reactivated before encoding Story 2 later incorporated significantly more accessory details from Story 2 into their recall of Story 1 than participants who encoded Story 2 without prior reactivation. In contrast, reminder-only reactivation was associated with better preservation and fewer distortions. These effects were expressed primarily in free recall. Thus, prior reactivation was associated with greater incorporation of information from a subsequent independent episode into the original memory.

title: A novel coumarin-derived Schiff base ligand suppresses TLR-NFκB signalling and oxidative stress in vitro, and exhibits anticonvulsant activity in vivo.
abstract: Neuroinflammation is a primary hallmark of chronic neurodegenerative diseases and is also implicated in poor outcomes following acute trauma and brain injury. Neuroinflammation arises largely from dysregulated activation of microglia, which disrupts neuronal function and promotes degradation of the blood-brain barrier. This, in turn, accelerates progressive neurotoxicity that characterises these conditions. Most neurodegenerative diseases are marked by a paucity of disease-modifying therapies, reflecting the complex, multicellular and multifaceted nature of their pathology. This presents a major challenge to the development of universally effective treatments. Activation of Toll-like receptors (TLRs), particularly TLR2 and TLR4, is widely reported to be a key driver of neuroinflammatory processes in these disorders. Naturally occurring agents, including coumarins, have been shown to downregulate TLR signalling and exert antioxidant effects under a number of disease-relevant conditions. We have previously reported the synthesis of a novel family of coumarin-derived Schiff base ligands with robust copper-complexing properties. In this study, we explored the bioactivity of one such ligand, L4, in the context of neuroinflammatory diseases. In particular, we examined the impact of L4 on microglial activation and neurotoxicity in vitro and on survival and behaviour in zebrafish models of inflammation and neuronal stress in vivo. Our results revealed that L4 alleviated microglial inflammatory responses, likely through inhibition of the TLR-NFκB pathway. In addition, L4 conferred protection against oxidative stress-induced neurotoxicity and produced an anticonvulsant effect in a zebrafish seizure model. Taken together, our findings support further investigation of L4 as a potential multitarget therapeutic for neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Repeated cocaine exposure and prolonged withdrawal drive morphological and molecular remodeling of hippocampal microglia in response to acute stress.
abstract: Repeated cocaine exposure during adolescence disrupts physiological brain maturation, inducing persistent neuroplastic adaptations that evolve throughout withdrawal. Because stressful experiences are among the most powerful triggers of relapse during abstinence, uncovering how cocaine withdrawal affects the neurobiological mechanisms of stress adaptation and emotional responses remains a critical challenge in addiction research. Here, we investigated whether prolonged withdrawal from adolescent cocaine exposure alters hippocampal neuroimmune responses to a subsequent stressful challenge. Male adolescent rats received cocaine (5mg/kg, s.c.) for 15 consecutive days followed by a 14-day withdrawal period. At the end of withdrawal, animals were exposed to acute restraint stress (ARS) and assessed for anxiety-like behavior. Our findings demonstrate that prolonged withdrawal from adolescent cocaine exposure impairs emotional adaptation to acute stress, accompanied by persistent neuroimmune dysregulation across both central and peripheral compartments. Within the hippocampus, a key limbic hub integrating contextual drug-associated memories, emotional processes and stress adaptation, cocaine withdrawal altered microglial homeostasis while reshaping stress-responsive neuro-glial communication pathways in a region-specific manner, particularly the CX3CL1-CX3CR1 axis within the ventral subregion. Stress exposure revealed distinct microglial and synaptic, structural and molecular, adaptations in cocaine-withdrawn rats, characterized by the recruitment of a surveillance-like microglial phenotype and an altered pattern of neuron-microglia communication. These central alterations were accompanied by peripheral lymphopenia and a blunted lymphocyte response to the challenge. Together, these findings support the existence of a latent neuroimmune vulnerability induced by cocaine withdrawal that becomes apparent under challenging conditions potentially driving maladaptive stress processing.

title: Oxidative stress in major depressive disorder: from experimental models to clinical therapeutic perspectives.
abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a highly prevalent psychiatric condition with complex and multifactorial pathophysiology. Increasing evidence suggests that oxidative stress, defined as an imbalance between reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and antioxidant defense systems, plays a central role in the onset and progression of MDD. This narrative review integrates findings from preclinical animal models, clinical studies and therapeutic interventions to provide a comprehensive overview of oxidative stress in MDD. Compared with healthy controls, patients with MDD consistently exhibit increased lipid peroxidation products, protein and DNA oxidation markers, and altered antioxidant defenses, including glutathione and superoxide dismutase. Animal models including chronic unpredictable mild stress, chronic social defeat stress, and lipopolysaccharide administration consistently demonstrate that oxidative stress drives depressive-like behaviors through mechanisms affecting dendritic spine density, glutamatergic function, and hippocampal neurogenesis. Additionally, oxidative stress is closely linked to inflammatory signaling and redox-regulatory signaling pathways, such as NF-κB and Nrf2/Keap1, highlighting its function as a major modulator of neuronal dysfunction in MDD. Therapeutic strategies targeting oxidative stress and spanning from conventional antidepressants to antioxidant compounds, stem cell therapies, natural products, and physical exercise demonstrate promising potential in restoring redox balance and improving depressive symptoms, although high heterogeneity across studies has been reported. Collectively, these findings support oxidative stress as a unifying mechanism in MDD pathophysiology and a promising target for novel diagnostic and therapeutic approaches.

title: MDMA-Assisted Therapy for Veterans with Comorbid Posttraumatic Stress Disorder and Alcohol Use Disorder: Clinical Outcomes from the First Open-Label Pilot Trial.
abstract: Co-occurring posttraumatic stress disorder and alcohol use disorder (PTSD-AUD) are highly prevalent among U.S. Veterans and associated with greater symptom severity, functional impairment, and poorer outcomes than either disorder alone. Existing treatments demonstrate modest effectiveness, with persistent challenges in engagement, retention, and sustained improvement. To evaluate the feasibility, safety, tolerability, and preliminary clinical outcomes of investigational 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA)-assisted therapy for Veterans with comorbid PTSD-AUD. We conducted the first open-label trial of MDMA-assisted therapy in Veterans (N = 10) with PTSD-AUD. The intervention included 11 therapy sessions (three preparatory, two MDMA assisted therapy sessions, and six integration), followed by a 4-week follow-up. Primary outcomes were PTSD symptom severity and alcohol consumption, measured by the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale for DSM-5 (CAPS-5) and Timeline Follow-Back (TLFB). Secondary outcomes assessed safety and tolerability. Exploratory outcomes included alcohol craving and substance misuse. Recruitment and retention were strong with 90% of enrolled participants completing treatment. MDMA-assisted therapy was associated with significant reductions in PTSD symptoms (p = 0.006, d = 1.241). Descriptive reductions were observed in alcohol consumption, including a 31% reduction in drinks per drinking day and a 54% reduction in heavy drinking days, although these changes did not reach clinical significance. No serious adverse events were reported. Treatment-emergent adverse events were non-serious and consistent with expected acute MDMA effects under protocol monitoring. Substance-use measures did not indicate systematic increases in alcohol or other substance use; one participant reported an isolated recurrence of cocaine use. Findings support the safety, feasibility, and tolerability of MDMA-assisted therapy and provide preliminary descriptive evidence of improvement in PTSD symptoms and alcohol-related outcomes. Larger randomized controlled trials are needed to evaluate efficacy, durability, and benefit-risk profile in this population.

title: The metabolic-brain axis: GLP-1 signaling, insulin resistance, and obesity pharmacotherapy in neurodegeneration.
abstract: The intersection of metabolic disease and neurodegeneration represents one of the most consequential frontiers in translational neuroscience. Converging epidemiological, mechanistic, and pharmacological evidence supports a bidirectional metabolic-brain axis in which systemic insulin resistance, obesity, and chronic metabolic inflammation are associated with and may contribute to alterations in neuronal survival, synaptic plasticity, and neuroimmune homeostasis. GLP-1 receptor agonists, originally developed for glycemic control and weight management, have therefore been investigated as potential disease-modifying therapies across Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and related neurodegenerative conditions through mechanisms including neuronal PKA activation, microglial NLRP3 suppression, mitochondrial biogenesis, and restoration of AQP4 perivascular localization that may contribute to glymphatic waste clearance. Direct human evidence for these CNS mechanisms remains limited or absent, with current support derived primarily from preclinical models and indirect human data, as detailed in Table 1, warranting dedicated investigation in the context of GLP-1 receptor agonism. Importantly, the two pivotal phase 3 programs designed to test this hypothesis in humans - EVOKE/EVOKE+ in early Alzheimer's disease and Exenatide-PD3 in Parkinson's disease - have both now reported, and neither demonstrated a statistically significant benefit on its primary clinical endpoint, despite favorable biomarker and epidemiological signals preceding these results. This review synthesizes current knowledge on brain insulin signaling, GLP-1 neurobiology, obesity-driven neuroinflammation, and the translational evidence for metabolic therapeutics in neurodegeneration, and uses the dissociation between mechanistic plausibility, epidemiological association, and null confirmatory trial results to identify critical knowledge gaps and translational barriers related to CNS target engagement, optimal dosing, and disease-modifying efficacy of GLP-1 receptor agonists. The review is organized into four major themes: brain insulin signaling, central GLP-1 biology, obesity-associated neuroinflammation, and the translational evidence supporting metabolic therapies for neurodegenerative disease.

title: Basics of Ultrasound for Transcranial Therapeutics Purposes.
abstract: Transcranial focused ultrasound therapy emerged as a uniquely versatile modality for non-invasive neuromodulation for the treatment of a range of neurological conditions and neuropsychiatric disorders. This work is intended to provide practitioners with fundamental background information directly relevant to the current application in this field, allowing them to critically interpret the literature and understand the technical and methodological considerations that underlie device operation, treatment planning and study parameter evaluation.

CLINICAL CHARACTERISTICS AND OUTCOMES IN ADULTS WITH BACTERIAL MENINGITIS AND NEGATIVE CEREBROSPINAL FLUID CULTURES.
abstract: Ten to thirty percent of patients with bacterial meningitis have negative CSF cultures, yet their clinical characteristics and outcome remain poorly defined. Between 2006 and 2023, adults with bacterial meningitis were prospectively included in a nationwide cohort study. Patients with negative CSF cultures were compared to those with positive CSF cultures. Outcome was assessed using the Glasgow Outcome Scale, with scores of 1-4 classified as unfavourable. CSF samples from microbiology-negative patients underwent additional testing with the IS-pro assay, a broad-spectrum PCR technique. CSF cultures were negative in 413 of 3,132 episodes (13%). A pathogen was identified in 328 (80%) through blood culture, CSF bacterial PCR, or antigen testing, leaving 85 episodes without microbiological confirmation. Patients with negative CSF cultures more often received pre-admission antibiotics (13% vs 10%, p=0.02) and had lower rates of unfavourable outcome (29% vs 39%, p<0.001). Blood cultures were positive in 53%, and CSF PCR detected a pathogen in 49%. The IS-pro assay detected Streptococcus pneumoniae (n=5), Streptococcus bovis group/Streptococcus intermedius (n=5), and Streptococcus constellatus (n=1). Bacterial meningitis patients with negative CSF cultures have more favourable outcomes. Combining CSF cultures with blood cultures and CSF PCR improves pathogen detection, while broad-spectrum PCR may help identify atypical pathogens.

title: Recent Advances in Immunomodulatory Biomaterial Strategies for Neural Tissue Healing.
abstract: Central and peripheral nervous system injuries represent major causes of neurological disability worldwide, yet current treatment methods are limited by issues including donor site morbidity, regenerative capacity, and tissue availability. Engineered biomaterials are being investigated as alternative strategies for neural tissue repair, but their regenerative efficacy remains variable, in part because of unresolved neuroinflammation and immune-mediated fibrous tissue formation. This review highlights immunomodulation as an important consideration beyond conventional biocompatibility and focuses on macrophage and microglial responses as key components of biomaterial-mediated neural repair. Here we start by outlining the distinct immunological landscapes of central and peripheral neural injury. We then examine how intrinsic material properties including stiffness, porosity, surface chemistry, electrical characteristics, and fiber alignment can influence immune cell behavior. Within this framework, we survey recent preclinical studies of major biomaterial platforms and distinguish, where experimental controls permit, intrinsic material-mediated effects from those produced by incorporated therapeutic cargos. Finally, we discuss the field's inconsistent phenotyping standards, reliance on rodent models, and common failure to assess long-term immunogenicity. Progress toward translation will require rigorous multi-marker characterization of immune-cell states, tissue- and injury-specific interpretation, standardized longitudinal assessment, and stronger integration of immunological outcomes with regenerative and functional endpoints. Collectively, these considerations position immunomodulation as a central design principle for the development of biomaterials for neural tissue repair. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Neural injuries often fail to heal because inflammation persists and implanted materials can promote scar formation. This review moves beyond describing biomaterials as simply biocompatible by evaluating how their physical and chemical properties actively shape macrophage and microglial behavior. By comparing recent strategies across peripheral and central nervous system repair, we identify immune-cell polarization as a central design target and examine how stiffness, porosity, alignment, surface chemistry, degradation, and therapeutic cargo influence healing. We also highlight major limitations in the literature, including inconsistent immune markers, limited long-term testing, and reliance on rodent models. This framework can guide the development of safer, more effective neural repair materials while improving the rigor and clinical relevance of future studies.

title: Nanotechnology-enabled Bromocriptine Delivery for Parkinson's Disease: Overcoming Pharmacokinetic Barriers and Advancing Brain Targeting.
abstract: Bromocriptine (BRC) is a semi-synthetic ergot alkaloid and potent dopamine D2 receptor agonist used to manage a variety of dopamine dysfunction disorders. Over the past few decades, BRC has been used therapeutically for metabolic, endocrinological, and neurological disorders. Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder in which dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra degenerate, depleting the striatum of dopamine. Globally, PD affects nearly 1% of individuals over 60 years of age, with its prevalence increasing as age advances. BRC exerts its therapeutic effects primarily through stimulation of dopamine D2 receptors, thereby modulating dopaminergic signalling and reducing the functional consequences of dopamine depletion. BRC could be used alone or as an adjunct with levodopa to reduce levodopa-induced dyskinesia and motor fluctuations. However, BRC has significant pharmacokinetic limitations, including poor oral absorption (28%) and low bioavailability (6%), due to its high lipophilicity, plasma protein binding, and first-pass metabolism. A comprehensive literature search was carried out using databases including PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar (January 2008-June 2026) using various keywords such as 'bromocriptine', 'nanoparticle', 'nanoformulation', 'blood-brain barrier', and 'Parkinson's disease' to identify and critically appraise bromocriptine-specific nanocarrier studies. In order to overcome the challenges associated with BRC delivery, nanoformulations have emerged as promising drug-delivery strategies. Lipid-based nanoparticles, including solid lipid nanoparticles and nanostructured lipid carriers, have shown potential to improve drug bioavailability. Numerous studies have shown that nanoemulsions have improved solubility and overcome brain targeting challenges. However, clinical studies are needed to determine whether the benefits observed with these nanoformulations can translate into clinically meaningful outcomes.

title: Within-state transcriptional remodelling predominates in a 41-gene ageing programme of human prefrontal OPCs.
abstract: Ageing impairs oligodendrocyte precursor cell (OPC) function, but it is unclear whether age-related transcriptional changes in the human cortex mainly reflect shifts in OPC-state composition or remodelling within transcriptionally defined states. We defined a bidirectional 41-gene OPC ageing programme (22 age-down and 19 age-up genes) and tested it in two external cortical single-nucleus datasets that were not used for gene selection. The age-down and age-up components showed the expected associations in each dataset. In paired RNA-chromatin profiles from 349 donors, formal decomposition showed that within-state change accounted for 98.8-99.5% of the programme's adjusted cell-mean contrast, whereas composition accounted for 0.8-1.2% under the primary clustering configuration; composition point estimates remained approximately 2% or less across five clustering resolutions and three representations. The relative occupancy of a commitment-associated OPC state declined with age in both donor sources after adjustment for sampled OPC depth, but removing this state left the broad programme essentially unchanged. Promoter accessibility changed in parallel with the RNA programme and correlated with paired RNA scores. The decomposition applies to the adjusted contrast of this 41-gene programme, and the occupancy estimate describes sampled OPC nuclei rather than absolute tissue abundance. Together, the results distinguish transcriptional remodelling distributed across OPC states from a focused change in commitment-associated state representation.

title: Glia proliferation and heterogeneity in CMT1A: Involvement of RUNX2-Schwann cells and endoneurial fibroblasts.
abstract: Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 1 A (CMT1A) is the most common inherited peripheral neuropathy, caused by duplication of the peripheral myelin protein 22 (PMP22) gene and characterized by dysmyelination and defects in myelin maturation. Hypercellularity, defined as an abnormal increase in the number of cells within a tissue, is a prominent feature of the disease, although its origin, persistence, and underlying mechanisms remain controversial. Here, we performed a time-course analysis of sciatic nerves from wild-type (WT) and CMT1A rats between 2 and 12 months of age. We demonstrated that CMT1A nerves exhibit persistent cellular proliferation extending into adulthood. This phenotype is confirmed by bulk RNA-seq data showing sustained enrichment of proliferation-associated gene signatures. Cell-type signature analysis identifies overrepresentation of immature, neural crest-related, and epithelial-mesenchymal transitional (EMT) transcriptional programs in CMT1A nerves. Among the most upregulated genes, RUNX2 showed strong and prolonged expression at both transcript and protein levels. Consistently with the key role of RUNX2 in the activation of the injury response, CMT1A nerves also showed a marked enrichment both in SOX10+/JUN+ cells and in SOX10+/RUNX2+ cells, indicating a maladaptive activation of the injury-like Schwann cell (SC) program. Interestingly, we detected robust upregulation of SMOC2, an extracellular matrix protein selectively expressed by endoneurial fibroblasts, pointing to activation of non-canonical cell types and altered extracellular matrix remodeling. Together, these data demonstrate that CMT1A peripheral nerves are characterized by chronic hypercellularity associated with persistent proliferation, EMT, and dysregulated injury transcriptional programs, collectively pointing at progressive and multicellular nerve remodeling as a relevant pathomechanism in the disease.

title: Targeting lipid peroxidation-derived aldehydes in Parkinson's Disease and ageing: Antioxidant investigations and mechanistic insights.
abstract: Oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation are increasingly recognized as age-related drivers of neurodegeneration, with Parkinson's disease (PD) representing a condition of heightened vulnerability. Among lipid peroxidation products, reactive aldehydes including 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal, malondialdehyde, acrolein, 4-hydroxy-2-hexenal, and crotonaldehyde have emerged not only as biomarkers of oxidative damage, but also as active mediators of neuronal dysfunction. Owing to their electrophilic nature, these aldehydes interact with nucleophilic residues, including cysteine, lysine, and histidine, forming covalent adducts that impair proteostasis, mitochondrial function, and redox signaling. Under physiological conditions, lipid peroxidation-derived aldehydes (LPDAs) are detoxified through glutathione-dependent conjugation and oxidoreductase-mediated metabolism. However, ageing progressively impairs these protective systems, promoting aldehyde accumulation and increasing dopaminergic vulnerability. We propose that PD may reflect, at least in part, an age-dependent impairment of aldehyde detoxification in addition to increased reactive oxygen species production. Although current experimental and clinical evidence supports the pathogenic relevance of some LPDAs in PD, antioxidant-based interventions have yielded inconsistent clinical outcomes. Within this framework, antioxidant strategies can be interpreted according to their functional impact on aldehyde burden. Approaches aimed at restoring glutathione homeostasis or activating Nrf2-dependent pathways may enhance endogenous detoxification systems and thereby support aldehyde clearance. More directly targeted approaches include strategies that enhance aldehyde metabolism, such as pharmacological activation of ALDH2. Overall, shifting the therapeutic focus from radical scavenging to the modulation of aldehyde burden through combined upstream and downstream interventions represents a promising but still underexplored avenue in PD and age-related neurodegenerative disorders that warrants further validation in clinical settings.

title: Effects of psilocybin with psychological support on anhedonia in treatment-resistant depression: A randomized controlled pilot trial.
abstract: Anhedonia is a core feature of major depressive disorder (MDD) that is frequently resistant to available treatments. Psilocybin's specific efficacy for anhedonia remains unclear. To evaluate psilocybin's efficacy for anhedonia in treatment-resistant MDD. In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 20 participants with treatment-resistant MDD received psilocybin (25 mg or 1 mg) with psychological support. The primary outcome was change in the Dimensional Anhedonia Rating Scale (DARS) score at week 1; DARS change at week 8 was a secondary outcome. The Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale (SHAPS) and Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) were used as additional secondary outcome measures for anhedonia and overall depression severity, respectively. The primary outcome was not statistically significant: between-group difference in DARS change at week 1 was 11.2 (95% confidence interval [CI], -1.0 to 23.3; p = 0.073). At week 8, the secondary DARS outcome indicated greater improvement in anhedonia with 25 mg (difference, 14.7; 95% CI, 2.5 to 26.8; p = 0.018). SHAPS improvement favored 25 mg at week 1 (difference, -3.2; 95% CI, -6.1 to -0.3; p = 0.029), but not week 8 (-2.1; 95% CI, -4.9 to 0.9; p = 0.168). MADRS improvement favored 25 mg at weeks 1 (-11.9; 95% CI, -19.2 to -4.5; p = 0.002) and 8 (-11.6; 95% CI, -19.0 to -4.2; p = 0.002). Psilocybin 25 mg did not significantly improve anhedonia at the primary week 1 endpoint. However, improvements on secondary measures suggest potential benefits for anhedonia and depression severity that warrant confirmation in larger trials. ClinicalTrials.govNCT06230757.

title: Governing artificial intelligence for reliable research.
Metabolic endotyping for mechanism-informed Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease trials.
abstract: Metabolically targeted therapies for Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease have yielded mixed results despite convergent evidence implicating three interconnected axes of metabolic dysfunction: insulin signaling, cellular bioenergetics, and lipid-lysosomal biology. We argue that this pattern partly reflects a trial-design problem: therapeutics such as glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists, terazosin, and stearoyl-CoA desaturase inhibitors generally have been tested in biologically unselected populations, with endpoints often distal to the targeted mechanism. We propose as a testable hypothesis that a metabolic endotype-a measurable, biomarker-supported pattern of metabolic dysfunction-spans subsets of both diseases and that failure to enrich for this endotype could dilute therapeutic signals in all-comer trials. We outline a modular four-tier framework integrating prodromal risk, metabolic vulnerability, pathway-specific confirmation, and mechanistic deep phenotyping to make Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease trials more interpretable and therapeutically informative.

title: The neurobiology of menopause: Implications for brain aging and Alzheimer's risk.
abstract: A growing body of evidence implicates the menopausal transition as a neurobiological inflection point in women's brain aging and Alzheimer's disease (AD) vulnerability. Menopause is a midlife neuroendocrine transition characterized by a decline in sex steroid hormones and widespread systemic effects. The brain is not a passive recipient of ovarian hormones but an active endocrine-sensing organ. Menopause, however, does not act in isolation: the ovarian-brain axis is established embryonically, activated at puberty, remodeled during pregnancy and postpartum, and reconfigured during the menopausal transition, with implications for later-life brain aging. This review places menopause within a lifespan neuroendocrine framework, examining mechanisms by which the transition may influence the brain, including altered hormone signaling, bioenergetics, synaptic plasticity, neurovascular function, inflammation, and AD-related pathology. It then reviews evidence linking menopausal timing to neurobiological and AD vulnerability, discusses estrogen therapy, and considers menopause as a biologically plausible window for risk stratification and prevention.

title: ERIS2: A deep-learning platform for predicting mutation-induced protein stability changes.
abstract: Accurately predicting changes in protein thermodynamic stability upon mutation is a fundamental challenge in protein engineering and therapeutics. Deep learning has improved prediction, but many models remain limited by small, imbalanced training data and poor generalization across mutation types. Here, we present ERIS2, an attention-convolutional deep learning framework that integrates contextual sequence embeddings with atomistic and residue-level structural features from experimental protein structures to predict mutation-induced stability changes. Trained on large-scale experimental measurements combined with curated ProTherm data, a 5-fold ERIS2 ensemble achieved Pearson correlation coefficients of 0.69 on S461, 0.51 on S669, and 0.60 on S96, three blind-test datasets sequence-disjoint from all training configurations, and showed negligible anti-symmetry bias on Ssym forward and reverse pairs. ERIS2 is freely available as a structure-based web server without registration, providing a robust framework for protein stability prediction and advancing computational tools for protein engineering and therapeutic design.

title: Age-dependent structural evolution of a functional amyloid contributes to memory impairment in Drosophila.
abstract: Cryogenic electron microscopy has revealed endpoint structures of ex vivo amyloid filaments, but how amyloids assemble and evolve in living organisms-and how these transitions affect physiology-remains poorly understood. Here, we map the age-dependent structural landscape of Orb2 amyloid, a synaptic translation regulator required for long-term memory, across the adult lifespan of Drosophila melanogaster. By determining multiple Orb2 amyloid structures, we uncover a dynamic, age-linked progression of amyloid states. Translation-promoting assemblies predominate early in life, whereas aging shifts the Orb2 amyloid ensemble toward structurally distinct, destabilization-resistant assemblies with reduced translational activity, coinciding with memory impairment. Manipulating memory-related chaperones in the brain shifts Orb2 toward youthful, translation-promoting states and improves memory in old flies; conversely, shifting Orb2 toward aged-like, translation-deficient states in young adults is associated with premature memory impairment. These findings define an in vivo trajectory of amyloid evolution and link amyloid structural dynamics to synaptic translation and memory.

title: Prospective associations between childhood stress characteristics and prenatal cortisol response to stress.
abstract: Maternal hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis functioning has important implications for maternal and offspring health, yet findings on cortisol responsivity to acute stress during pregnancy are mixed. Further, little is known about how childhood stress exposure relates to physiological stress regulation during this period, particularly among Black and White women. The present study leveraged multiple waves of prospectively gathered data from a large population-based sample to examine associations between degree of exposure to subsistence-, safety- and caregiving-related stress across childhood and cortisol responsivity during a later pregnancy. Participants (N = 338, 69.7% Black, 26.7% White) were enrolled in the longitudinal Pittsburgh Girls Study in middle childhood. Caregivers reported annually on exposure to a range of stressors when participants were 7-17 years of age. During a prenatal laboratory visit in which participants were between 22 and 31 years of age, participants completed the Trier Social Stress Test (TSST) and provided saliva samples for cortisol assay. Adjusting for covariates, the TSST did not produce a significant increase in cortisol levels over time, though 28.3% of participants were classified as responders. Greater exposure to subsistence-related stress (e.g., resource strain, housing instability) across childhood was associated with blunted cortisol levels during pregnancy. Findings suggest that childhood exposure to subsistence-related stress may have enduring effects on physiological stress regulation and underscore the potential value of targeted preventive interventions to promote intergenerational health. Results also highlight the relevance of public health initiatives aimed at reducing population-level differences in subsistence-related stress exposure.

title: Psychological resilience is associated with increased heterogeneity in the clinical aging phenotypes of patients with cancer.
abstract: Cancer and its treatments are associated with accelerated aging. Emerging evidence suggests that patients' self-reports of symptoms, functional status, and resilience can identify clinical aging phenotypes. The purpose was to identify distinct clinical aging phenotypes using: six (evening fatigue, sleep disturbance, depression, state anxiety, cognitive function, physical function); seven (addition of pain); and eight (addition of resilience) clinical indicators and evaluate for differences in patient characteristics and quality of life (QOL) outcomes among the phenotypes. Outpatients (n = 1340) completed questionnaires prior to their second or third cycle of chemotherapy. Three separate latent variable models using six, seven, and eight clinical indicators were created. Differences among phenotypes in demographic and clinical characteristics and QOL outcomes were evaluated using parametric and non-parametric tests. Determination of clinically meaningful differences in QOL scores was done using Cohen's d. For the six and seven indicator models, two and three distinct phenotypes were identified, respectively. For the eight indicator model, five distinct phenotypes were identified: Very Low (32.6%), Low (32.2%), Moderate (16.4%), High (13.2%), and Very High (5.6%) clinical age. Being female, younger, having a higher comorbidity burden, and lower functional status were associated with the worst clinical aging profiles. QOL scores decreased in a stepwise fashion and differences were clinically meaningful. Inclusion of a measure of psychological resilience in the model allows for better discrimination of inter-individual variability in clinical aging phenotypes of oncology outpatients. This approach may assist with identification of patients at increased risk for accelerated aging.

title: Understanding the lived experience of epilepsy through creative engagement workshops: Insights beyond patient-generated questions.
abstract: Questions tell us what people with epilepsy want to know, but not what they live through. Building on previous analyses of patient-generated questions about epilepsy, this study explored whether creative engagement workshops illuminate the lived experiences that underlie information-seeking. We explored whether this approach could provide insights to guide the design of digital and other support resources that better meet patients' needs. Twenty-two participants (12 adults with epilepsy and 10 carers/family members) attended two co-facilitated creative engagement workshops. Qualitative data from creative outputs, facilitated discussions, field notes and evaluation feedback were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Findings were interpreted alongside a previous analysis of 2,752 epilepsy-related questions submitted to online forums. Two lived-experience themes emerged: living with uncertainty and adaptation and identity. Participants described uncertainty about seizures as a pervasive influence on daily life, while many discussed adapting to epilepsy and maintaining independence and identity. Family members highlighted the broader impact on carers and family life. Peer connection and shared discussion during the workshops were consistently valued, with many describing reduced isolation and increased validation through contact with others affected by epilepsy. Patient-generated questions identify information needs, whereas creative engagement methods illuminate the emotional and social experiences in daily life underlying those needs. This richer understanding can guide the development of more authentic and patient-centred care. The development of online versions of the creative workshops is now underway, aiming to extend access to the benefits observed in this pilot study.

title: Clinical correlates of complete versus partial remission in major depressive disorder: an exploratory analysis of three cohorts.
journal: European neuropsychopharmacology : the journal of the European College of Neuropsychopharmacology
abstract: Remission in major depressive disorder (MDD) is conventionally defined as a 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD-17) score ≤7, but patients within this range may retain residual symptoms. We explored whether complete remission (HAMD-17 <4) and partial remission (HAMD-17 4-7) differ in baseline clinical features, symptom trajectories and endpoint functioning. Three cohorts were analysed separately: GSRD (N=2583, cross-sectional, tertiary centres), PANDORA (N=215, week 12) and STAR*D level 1 (N=1565). We estimated effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals, false discovery rate (FDR) correction, adjusted and imputed models, alternative cut-offs, individual symptom trajectories and cross-validated discrimination. Baseline differences between complete and partial remitters were small (median absolute standardized difference 0.08-0.15). No baseline variable survived FDR correction; only a concurrent severe-episode rating in GSRD did (odds ratio 2.10, 95% CI 1.43-3.07). In STAR*D, partial remitters had slightly higher baseline HAMD-17 (g=0.15, 95% CI 0.00-0.31), and most item-level associations were explained by overall severity. Baseline features did not discriminate the groups in individual patients (cross-validated AUC 0.42-0.55). Symptom scores of the two groups separated within 4-6 weeks and did not converge during follow-up. In STAR*D, the estimated rate of improvement did not differ detectably, and the model-estimated asymptote was higher in partial remitters. At STAR*D exit, partial remitters had worse work and social adjustment (g=0.45) and quality of life (g=-0.63) despite similar baseline values. Complete and partial remission identify different endpoint states, but baseline clinical features predict this distinction poorly. These exploratory findings require prospective confirmation.

title: T-cell engagers in small-cell lung cancer: current evidence and future directions - a position statement from the ETOP IBCSG Partners Foundation Workshop.
abstract: T-cell engagers (TCEs) are a novel class of immunotherapeutic molecules that enhance immune responses to cancer by directing T cells to target tumour cells. Tumour-associated antigens have been identified for several solid malignancies, including delta-like ligand 3 (DLL3) for small-cell lung cancer (SCLC). Several DLL3-targeted TCEs are being developed for the treatment of SCLC, including tarlatamab, gocatamig and obrixtamig. Tarlatamab is approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration and represents a new standard of care in patients with pretreated SCLC. As experience with TCEs in SCLC increases, consensuses on optimal clinical settings and patient management are evolving. Rapid identification and effective management of potentially life-threatening immune-related side-effects, such as cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS), are essential for successful treatment with TCEs. Here we briefly review the key studies of TCEs in development for solid tumours before providing a comprehensive discussion on the clinical management of TCE therapy in patients with SCLC. We consider issues related to clinical settings, patient evaluation and management of toxicities, with a particular focus on identification and treatment of CRS and ICANS, drawing on experience from other oncology settings. TCEs represent a transformative treatment option for SCLC, offering new hope for a disease traditionally associated with poor therapeutic outcomes. TCEs also, however, bring new challenges, including the effective management of immune-related side-effects and the logistical demands of treatment. Safe implementation will depend on robust infrastructure, multidisciplinary collaboration, and patient and caregiver education.

title: Predictors of quality of life in older adults with major psychiatric disorders: A prospective multicenter study.
abstract: Quality of life (QoL) in older adults with major psychiatric disorders is affected by various clinical and social factors, yet longitudinal evidence on QoL determinants remains limited. This study tests a comprehensive model of predictors of QoL using structural equation modelling (SEM). We analysed data from the Cohort of individuals with Schizophrenia Aged 55 years or more (CSA) study, a multicenter cohort of older adults diagnosed with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, or major depressive disorder, recruited from 63 French psychiatric centers. QoL was assessed using the Quality-of-Life Scale (QLS) at baseline and follow-up (median = 3.0 years, SD = 1.44). We examined the simultaneous effects on QLS at follow-up of six predictor groups assessed at baseline, including (1) severity of general psychopathology, (2) severity of depressive symptoms, (3) severity of cognitive impairment, (4) psychotropic medications, (5) general medical conditions, and (6) sociodemographic characteristics. Six predictors showed significant independent longitudinal associations with QoL. Lower QoL was associated with greater depressive symptoms (β=-0.225), greater cognitive impairment (β=-0.117), antipsychotic polypharmacy (β=-0.538) and longer follow-up (β=-0.330) (all p-values<0.05). In contrast, higher baseline QoL (β=0.401) and greater levels of general psychopathology (β=0.291) were positively associated with follow-up QoL. Depression, cognitive impairment and antipsychotic polypharmacy emerged as markers of poorer QoL, independently of baseline QoL and diagnosis, although the association with depression was not robust in sensitivity analyses. The unexpected positive association with psychopathology is compatible with statistical suppression, measurement overlap, survival bias and limited illness awareness rather than a true benefit of symptoms.

title: Manganese exposure activates the cGAS-STING-IL-17 axis and is associated with Tau and α-synuclein accumulation in mice.
abstract: Excessive manganese (Mn) exposure is an environmental risk factor for neurodegeneration, yet the circuitry linking Mn‑induced innate immune activation to proteinopathy remains unclear. Here, by combining in vivo manganese chloride (MnCl2) exposure in mice with BV2 microglial models, we demonstrate that the cGAS-STING pathway promotes interleukin-17 (IL‑17)‑mediated neuroinflammation and neurotoxic protein accumulation. Mice administered MnCl2 in drinking water for five weeks showed elevated levels of Tau, phosphorylated Tau (p-Tau), and α-synuclein (α-Syn), along with activation of the cGAS-STING pathway (upregulated cGAS, STING, p‑STING, p‑IRF3), increased IL‑17 A and IL‑1β levels, and an increased proportion of differentially expressed genes from transcriptomic analysis annotated to the IL-17 pathway. In BV2 microglia, MnCl2 similarly activated cGAS-STING and upregulated IL‑17 A and IL‑1β. CRISPR‑mediated deletion of cGAS or STING abolished Mn‑induced STING-IRF3 phosphorylation, blunted IL‑17 pathway expression, and prevented the accumulation of Tau, p‑Tau, and α‑Syn. Neutralisation of IL‑17 A with a blocking antibody partially attenuated Mn‑induced Tau and α‑Syn upregulation. Molecular docking, co‑immunoprecipitation and molecular dynamics analyses suggested potential physical associations between IL‑17 A and both Tau and α‑Syn. Collectively, our findings implicate the cGAS-STING-IL-17 axis as a candidate pathway linking Mn-induced innate immune activation to neurodegeneration-related protein aggregation.

title: Positively valenced outcomes increase outcome binding in human-robot interaction.
abstract: Sense of agency (SoA) refers to the experience of being an agent who initiates actions and brings about their consequences. Prior work suggests that positive outcomes may produce a stronger sense of agency than negative outcomes and that predictability of outcome valence may modulate these differences. One approach used to investigate SoA is temporal binding. However, the measure can comprise two components, action binding and outcome binding, which appear to be dissociable and may depend on partly different cognitive mechanisms. In the present study, we examined whether positive outcomes strengthen binding relative to neutral outcomes and whether predictability affects the two components differently. Participants completed a Libet clock task in which a voluntary keypress caused the humanoid robot iCub to produce either a positive emotional vocalization or an acoustically similar neutral tone. iCub's facial expression indicated whether the valence of the upcoming sound was predictable or unpredictable. Positive vocalizations produced stronger outcome binding than neutral tones, whereas predictability did not reliably influence outcome binding or alter the effect of valence. Action binding was not significantly modulated by either valence or predictability. The two components were also not associated when measured across participants. These findings suggest that positive outcome valence can strengthen outcome binding relative to a neutral consequence, without a reliable change in action binding, and further support treating the two components of temporal binding separately.

title: Liposomal coating of near infrared resonant magnetic-plasmonic nanostars for blood-brain barrier-like passage, selective targeting, and bioorthogonal surface-enhanced Raman scattering imaging.
journal: Journal of colloid and interface science
abstract: A flexible phospholipid bilayer can conformally coat highly anisotropic iron oxide@gold nanostars (M@NSts), maintain colloidal stability over 7 days, and preserve magnetic manipulability and near-infrared (NIR) plasmonic properties. Embedding a hydrophobic bioorthogonal Raman reporter within the membrane should enable background-free surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) without prior immobilization on gold, while the biomimetic interface should promote endothelial transport and molecular targeting. The resulting modular architecture may also support future therapeutic cargo loading. Reduced-size iron oxide nanoflowers retaining their multicore magnetic architecture were decorated with gold seeds and grown into M@NSts. Reporter-loaded liposomes composed of 1,2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DOPC) and poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG)-conjugated 1,2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine bearing terminal carboxyl groups (DOPE-PEG-COOH) were osmotically ruptured and reassembled around the nanostars to form flexible, bioconjugatable coatings. Transwell assays compared lipid-coated and PEGylated M@NSts across endothelial colony-forming cell (ECFC) and blood-brain barrier (BBB)-relevant human brain microvascular endothelial cell (HBEC-5i) monolayers. Transport into the basolateral compartment was quantified by nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) and inductively coupled plasma atomic emission spectroscopy (ICP-AES), followed by magnetic enrichment and SERS analysis. Cholera toxin subunit B (CT-B)-mediated recognition of monosialotetrahexosylganglioside (GM1) was assessed. The optimized synthesis reduced nanoflower diameter from 130 ± 20 to 70 ± 10 nm while preserving magnetic responsiveness. The bilayer conformed to the spiky surface and preserved NIR plasmonic activity while positioning the reporter near gold for efficient SERS enhancement. The probes displayed a background-free band at 2218 cm-1 and remained colloidally and spectroscopically stable for seven days. Lipid-coated M@NSts showed 1.8- and 3.1-fold higher transport than PEGylated controls across ECFC and the more restrictive HBEC-5i monolayers, respectively. Basolateral SERS detection after magnetic enrichment supported preservation of the lipid-nanostar association. Enhanced transport occurred with moderate permeability changes but no significant monolayer disruption. As proof of concept, conjugation with CT-B promoted specific recognition of cellular GM1. The lipid interface therefore integrates stabilization, magnetic recovery, bioorthogonal detection, endothelial transport, and molecular targeting.

title: Rapid antidepressant effects of ketamine combined with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors: Mechanisms and outlook.
abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a prevalent and disabling psychiatric illness. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), while the cornerstone of first-line pharmacotherapy, are limited by delayed therapeutic onset and high rates of nonresponse or partial response. Our previous work demonstrated that a single subanesthetic dose of ketamine or its enantiomers can accelerate SSRI response and enhance efficacy in patients with residual fluctuations after initial improvement. We hypothesize that this combination is synergistic rather than merely additive, although the precise mechanisms remain to be fully characterized. Synthesizing these observations with a comprehensive literature review, we propose the GLIMPSE model (Glu-GABA Long-circuit Integrative Metaplasticity for Psychopathology and Synaptic Efficacy), an integrative framework positing that the dorsal raphe-prefrontal cortex 5-HT-glutamate/GABA circuit functions as an upstream driver, whereas metaplasticity and synaptic priming serve as the key downstream convergence points for ketamine-SSRI synergy. Building on this framework, we further outline a practical safety-monitoring protocol for serotonin syndrome associated with this combination, alongside a future-oriented research agenda grounded in the GLIMPSE model to guide subsequent mechanistic and clinical investigations.

title: Transcranial photobiomodulation mitigates anxiety and depression-like behavior by modulation of mitochondrial and neuroinflammatory pathways in a mouse model of simulated microgravity.
journal: Journal of photochemistry and photobiology. B, Biology
abstract: Mental health is a major concern for astronauts due to the high risk of anxiety and depression caused by prolonged exposure to microgravity and the stresses of spaceflight. Existing pharmacological treatments are inadequate for space missions, emphasizing the necessity for safe, noninvasive interventions. This study explored the therapeutic efficacy of transcranial photobiomodulation (tPBM) using near-infrared (NIR) light therapy on mood regulation and the neurobiological mechanisms in mice subjected to simulated microgravity. Male mice were divided into three groups: a control group, a hindlimb unloading (HU) group subjected to 28 days of unloading, and an HU + tPBM group receiving daily tPBM treatment at 810 nm. The forced swim and tail suspension tests were employed to evaluate depressive-like behavior, while the elevated plus maze and open field tests were employed to measure anxiety-like behavior. Biochemical analysis of prefrontal cortex samples assessed mitochondrial bioenergetics (cytochrome c oxidase subunit 5 A [Cox5A], NADH dehydrogenase activity, mitochondrial membrane potential, and ATP), oxidative stress markers (NADPH oxidase 2 [NOX2], reactive oxygen species [ROS], and antioxidant activity), as well as neuroinflammatory mediators (toll-like receptor 4 [TLR4], phosphorylated mitogen-activated protein kinase [p-MAPK], phosphorylated nuclear factor kappa-B [p-NF-κB], interleukin-1β, and interferon-γ). HU provoked behavior resembling anxiety and depression, along with increased corticosterone levels, compromised mitochondrial function, increased NOX2 and ROS levels, and activated TLR4/MAPK/NF-κB signaling. Notably, tPBM reversed these changes, restored mitochondrial bioenergetics, diminished oxidative stress, and suppressed neuroinflammation, leading to considerable behavioral improvement. These findings indicate that tPBM may represent a promising, non-invasive approach for ameliorating mental health issues during long-duration spaceflight.

title: Morpholine-Based Chalcones as Potent and Selective MAO-B Inhibitors With Preliminary CNS Drug-Like Properties.
abstract: A series of morpholine-based chalcone derivatives containing alkoxy substituents was designed and synthesized using a rapid and environmentally friendly microwave-assisted protocol. The synthesized compounds were fully characterised by NMR, FTIR, and HRMS analyses and evaluated in vitro against primarily monoamine oxidases, as well as acetylcholinesterase, butyrylcholinesterase, and β-site amyloid precursor protein cleaving enzyme 1, which are closely associated with neurodegenerative disorders. Although most compounds showed weak inhibition of AChE, BChE, and BACE1, they exhibited potent and selective MAO-B inhibitory activity. Among them, MBC21 emerged as the most potent MAO-B inhibitor (IC50 = 0.069 ± 0.0075 μM; SI 243.33), acting as a competitive and reversible inhibitor. In addition, MBC1, MBC2, and MBC24 displayed notable BChE inhibitory activity, while MBC24 demonstrated multi-target activity against MAO-B, AChE, and BChE. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations revealed that the selectivity of MBC21 towards hMAO-B is associated with stable hydrophobic interactions and π-π stacking with TYR326. Furthermore, in silico ADME prediction, microsomal stability, and PAMPA-BBB studies demonstrated favorable drug-like properties, improved metabolic stability, and moderate brain permeability for MBC21. Taken together, these findings identify MBCs, particularly MBC21, as promising lead candidates for the development of selective MAO-B inhibitors for neurodegenerative disease therapy.

title: Microbiome-based survey of pathogenic bacteria at the chimpanzee-human-livestock interface, Uganda.
abstract: Anthropogenic land-use change is intensifying contact among wildlife, humans, and livestock in tropical ecosystems, increasing opportunities for cross-species transmission of infectious agents. Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes schweinfurthii), owing to their close phylogenetic relationship with humans, are particularly susceptible to pathogen spillover. We performed a microbiome-based screening of potentially pathogenic bacteria in faecal samples from a chimpanzee-human-livestock interface in western Uganda using full-length 16S rRNA gene sequencing. A total of 21 bacterial genera, categorized as potentially pathogenic, were detected across all three studied host groups, from which several taxa of potential zoonotic or health relevance, including Clostridium perfringens, Salmonella enterica, Shigella spp., and Streptococcus suis, were detected in chimpanzees, humans, and goats. Our findings indicate an overlap in bacterial taxa across the interface. The relative abundance of potentially pathogenic bacterial taxa was descriptively lower in chimpanzees than in humans and livestock, but carried both enteric and respiratory bacterial species previously associated with disease outbreaks in captive and wild populations. These findings support integrating bacterial monitoring into conservation-oriented One Health frameworks.

title: Silencing las and rhl quorum sensing systems in MDR Pseudomonas aeruginosa: Design, synthesis, biological evaluation and molecular modeling of novel quinolin-2-one derivatives.
abstract: This study reports the design and synthesis of novel quinolin-2-one derivatives as bioisosteric analogues for native N-acyl homoserine lactones (AHLs) to fight multidrug-resistant (MDR) Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Among the synthesized compounds, the Schiff base derivative (6g) emerged as a potent lead, exhibiting a Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) of 1.25 μg/mL against MDR clinical isolate. Phenotypic assays demonstrated that sub-MIC concentrations of 6g reduced biofilm biomass by 92.30%. Time-kill analysis demonstrated concentration-dependent antibacterial activity, with 2× MIC producing 4.2-log10 CFU/mL reduction at 24 h, whereas the 1/2 MIC concentration used for the anti-virulence studies did not produce extensive bacterial killing. Quantitative RT-PCR revealed significant downregulation of the core QS genes lasR (94.72%), rhlR (91.65%), lasI (84.84%), and rhlI (76.46%). Importantly, functional evaluation using LasR-dependent β-galactosidase reporter assay demonstrated concentration-dependent LasR inhibition by 6g, with an IC50 of 0.62 ± 0.05 μM, providing experimental support for LasR-mediated QS interference. Molecular docking supported favorable accommodation of the active derivatives within the RhlR, RhlI, LasR, and LasI binding pockets offering a theoretical rationale for potential broad quorum-sensing interference, while SwissADME analysis computationally predicted limited blood-brain barrier penetration and a preliminary predicted ADME profile for 6g. Together with its low mammalian cytotoxicity and high selectivity index (SI ≈ 267), these findings identify 6g as a promising quinolin-2-one lead displaying combined antibacterial and QS-associated anti-virulence activity that warrants further biophysical target validation and in vivo investigation.

title: Design and synthesis of carvedilol-derived dual-functional adjuvant agents with oral activity against doxorubicin cardiotoxicity and anticancer efficacy.
abstract: Developing dual-functional agents that simultaneously exert potent antitumor effects and attenuate chemotherapy-induced cardiotoxicity represents a promising strategy in cancer adjuvant therapeutics. Herein, forty-six carvedilol (CAR) derivatives were designed and synthesized to potentiate neddylation-inhibitory anticancer potency and bioavailability, while retaining cardioprotective property originating from CAR. Among these, the optimal derivative 28 exhibited potent antiproliferative activity across multiple cancer cell lines, and mitigated cardiomyocyte injury. Mechanistically, 28 targets Nedd8-activating enzyme (NAE) to inhibit the neddylation pathway, thereby suppressing tumor growth in vitro and in vivo. In addition, 28 attenuates Doxorubicin (DOX)-induced cardiotoxicity via pleiotropic effects, mainly including β-AR antagonism and suppression of reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation. In tumor-bearing and DOX-induced heart failure mouse models, 28 enhances antitumor activity of DOX and mitigates its cardiotoxicity by oral administration. Overall, this study provides a reliable strategy for the development of novel adjuvant agents that concurrently suppress tumor progression and mitigate DOX-induced cardiotoxicity.
